the connection with the rest of the railroad must lie off to the right, and the
dead/stub end of the track lies off to the left. Both readings put the car on

## The inference

To be standing where it is, the car had to travel through the derail's location

the last movement was an inbound one: the train came from the right‑hand
(foreground) end of the track, moved away from the camera and to the left, and
stopped as soon as it was clear of the derail. The derail was then thrown back
onto the rail and locked behind it. That is exactly the state the photo shows,
and it is the standard sequence when cars are shoved into a siding, spur or
storage track and secured.

The opposite direction does not fit. Had the train been moving left to right,
i.e. toward the camera, the applied derail sitting right in front of the wheel
would have thrown that wheel off the rail rather than let the car come to a
tidy stop; and no crew deliberately brings a cut of cars to a stand a couple of
feet short of a locked derail. The only way the car could be where it is, with
the derail closed ahead of it, is that it went in past the derail first.

## Corroborating detail

The car has clearly been sitting for a long time — rust rings on the wheel
tread, rust and lichen on the rail, leaves and litter packed into the cribs and
against the rail, no bright wheel‑polished band on the railhead in either
direction. So this is stored equipment left secured behind a locked derail,
not a train that has merely paused. That fits the "shoved in and left" reading
rather than a movement still on its way somewhere.

## Statement of the answer

* Direction of travel before stopping: **leftwards in the image / away from the
  camera, from the foreground end of the track toward the distance.**
* Where it came from: **the right‑hand, near end of the track**, where the rails
  run past the photographer toward the connection with the rest of the railroad.
* In operating terms: **it was going into this track (a shove or pull in past the
  open derail), not coming out of it.** The derail now lying on the rail behind
  its wheel was restored and locked after the movement stopped.

The one thing that would overturn this is if the yellow block were not the fixed
hinged derail it appears to be but something laid on the rail afterwards; the
base plate bolted to the tie, the pivot pin, and the throw rod running back to
the target stand rule that out.

---

### 1. Identification of the Safety Equipment
* **The Yellow Derailer:** The yellow device sitting directly on the right-hand rail head is a **hinged derailer** (specifically, a single-rail sliding/hinged model, such as a Hayes EB derail). Its purpose is to intentionally derail any unauthorized or runaway rolling stock to prevent it from entering and fouling an active main track.
* **The Derail Operating Stand:** On the left foreground, there is a hand-operated switch stand connected to the yellow derailer via a metal tie rod running under the track.
* **The Vane/Target Signal:** The switch stand is equipped with a color-coded target. The **red circular target** is currently facing the camera (aligned with the track direction), which is the universal railroad signal indicating that the derailer is **active ("ON" the rail)**. The green pointed vanes are oriented perpendicular to the track.
* **The Padlock Security:** The operating lever of the switch stand is pressed down in its latch and **secured with a locked brass padlock**. This indicates that the derailer is locked in the active position to secure the track.

---

### 2. Siding vs. Main Line Orientation
* A derailer is always installed on a siding, industrial spur, or house track at the "clearance point" just before the track connects to an active main line.
* The derailer is designed to protect the main line from cars rolling out of the siding. This means:
  * The **siding/storage area** (where cars are safely parked) is located to the **left (background / deeper into the image)**.
  * The **main line** (which is being protected) is located to the **right (foreground / closer to the camera)**.
* Since the rail car's wheels are located to the left of the yellow derailer, the car is parked on the protected "siding" side of the device.

---

### 3. Reconstruction of the Last Movement (Right-to-Left)
To park the train car in its current storage position on the siding, the following standard railroad operating procedures had to be performed:
1. The train arrived from the main line, meaning it was positioned in the foreground/right.
2. A crew member had to walk to the switch stand, unlock the brass padlock, and throw the lever. This action pulled the tie rod and flipped the yellow derailer **off the rail** (to the open/inactive position) to clear the track.
3. The train was then shoved or pulled **from the right to the left** (from the foreground into the background, deeper into the siding) past the derailer location.
4. Once the rail car reached its final spot (where its wheels now rest, just to the left of the derailer), the train came to a stop, and its handbrakes were applied.
5. The locomotive uncoupled from the car and exited the siding (or remained on the main-line side of the derailer).
6. The crew member then returned to the switch stand, threw the lever to flip the yellow derailer back **onto the rail** (active position), and locked the brass padlock to secure the siding.
7. Therefore, the very last movement of this train before coming to a stop and being left here was from **right to left** (away from the camera, into the background).

---

### 4. Why the Alternative (Left-to-Right) is Impossible
If the train had been moving from left to right (from the background towards the foreground, out of the siding) before coming to a stop:
* **The Active Derailer Obstruction:** Since the derailer is currently locked in the active position on top of the rail, any movement from left to right would have resulted in the train running over the yellow block and derailing. Looking closely at the bogie/truck, the wheels are perfectly aligned on the rails and have not derailed.
* **Rust and Inactivity:** The heavy layer of orange-brown rust coating both the wheel treads and the rail heads indicates that this train car has been stationary in this exact spot for a very long period (weeks or months). If the train had stopped here during an active movement to exit the siding, the wheel treads and rails would be shiny/polished from recent friction, and the derailer would be unlocked and open rather than locked and active.
* **Emergency Stop Improbability:** If a train was moving from left to right and had to perform an emergency stop right before hitting the derailer, the train crew would be present, and the derailer would not be locked with a padlocked switch stand.

### Conclusion
Thus, the physical evidence of the **locked, active yellow derailer** situated to the right (foreground-ward) of the **heavily rusted wheels of the parked rail car** proves beyond doubt that the train's last movement before coming to a stop was **from right to left** (from the main-line direction/foreground into the siding/background, away from the camera).
